title: The farmer Guru
hook: Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur with his community (Sikh tradition)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita: whatever you do, eat or give, do it as an offering. Your line was as an offering. What task did you hand over? Day eight hundred ninety-four.

Visitors came to Kartarpur looking for a holy man, and Sikh tradition says they found a farmer. The fields lay in the Punjab. The man walking the furrow was a teacher people had traveled to hear. Tradition says that after years on the road, Guru Nanak, whose teaching began the Sikh path, settled at Kartarpur, a village tradition says he founded himself. And there he farmed. Those visitors found him working in the fields, then singing with everyone in the evening, then eating at the same shared meal. Today's word is that picture.
screen: `LOOKING FOR A HOLY MAN.` → `THEY FOUND A FARMER.` → `FIELDS, SONG, A SHARED MEAL.`

segments.voice: First, the shape of a day at Kartarpur, as tradition tells it. Hymns of praise in the early morning. Work in the fields through the day. Hymns again in the evening. And a shared kitchen where everyone ate together, whoever they were. Work and worship weren't two lives. They were one day. Second, the teaching behind it. Sikh teaching sums up the Guru's way in short phrases. Naam japna, remembering God's name. Vand chhakna, sharing what you have. And kirat karni, earning an honest living by your own work. The Guru Granth Sahib puts it in a line, in paraphrase: the one who eats what they earn by their own labor, and gives some of it away, knows the path. Third, the kind of life it pointed to. In the Guru's world, some seekers left their families and lived on what others gave them. Guru Nanak, as Sikhs remember him, taught his followers another way: stay in the world, marry, raise a family, work, share. A householder's life, lived with God in mind. Sikh teaching still holds up this ideal. Fourth, a story Sikhs tell from those fields. A seeker named Lehna came to Kartarpur and served the Guru. Tradition says that one day, in his good clothes, he carried a heavy bundle of wet grass from the fields on his head, and the mud ran down. He didn't mind. Lehna became the next Guru, Guru Angad. The Sikh line of Gurus, tradition says, passed on in a farmyard, not a throne room.
screen: `SONG, FIELDS, SONG, A SHARED MEAL.` · `REMEMBER, SHARE, EARN HONESTLY.` · `A HOUSEHOLDER'S LIFE.` · `LEHNA AND THE WET GRASS.` · then, large: `KIRAT KARNI.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind the people you live or work with. Family, housemates, coworkers, neighbors. Now think of one ordinary chore that you could do alongside one of them today, not for them, with them. Cooking, cleaning up, carrying something, weeding a patch of ground. Picture it: two pairs of hands on one job, the small talk, the finish. Breathe in the picture. Breathe out any idea that the chore is beneath you, or a waste of a day. If you pray, you can remember God's name in your own tradition's way while you sit. The bell holds the time.
The farmer Guru. Guru Nanak, as Sikh tradition remembers his last years: farming at Kartarpur, singing and eating with his community. Today's word.
Your line: the farmer guru. Today, do one chore alongside others: cook, clean or carry something together, side by side. Day eight hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of kirat karni, earning an honest living, alongside remembering God and sharing; at gurdwaras, volunteers cook, serve and clean the langar, the shared community kitchen.

what it means: Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak farming at Kartarpur, joining work, worship and a shared meal.
what a scholar hears: the householder ideal of kirat karni, and the Guru Granth Sahib's line that one who earns by labor and gives some away knows the path.

notes: Ang 1245 paraphrased (ghaal khaae kichh hathahu dei); confirm Ang number and paraphrase.

Lehna and the wet grass is told as a tradition story; a Sikh Keeper should confirm the details told (good clothes, mud).
'In the Guru's world, there were holy men who left their families and lived on what others gave them' is a general historical claim; confirm it doesn't frame any group unfairly.

Editor: hook now opens on the visitors' arrival instead of another fragment list ('Mud on the feet. A plow behind an ox.'), and drops the unsourced river and ox details; 'there were holy men who left their families' softened to 'some seekers', so renunciants aren't a foil; 'Sikhs often sum up' changed to avoid a sweeping 'often' claim.

Audit: hook said Nanak 'settled in this village' as if he arrived at an existing place; Sikh tradition says he founded Kartarpur, now stated as tradition. Cut 'didn't build a palace or a retreat on a hill' (an unsourced foil). Ang 1245 (ghaal khaae kichh hathahu dei) checks out.
